extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, scientists, educators, and reviewers interested in science, science education, and scholarly/book evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial commentary and literary notices evaluating standards for science education, the role of hypotheses in teaching, and criteria for judging scholarly and popular books (chemistry treatises, medical texts, histories, reference works, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virchow's swearing-test for school instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Can you make oath, gentlemen, to the truth of what you offer?" — the standard that only facts which can be sworn to (certainties up to the 'swearing-point') ought to be admitted into schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors argue this standard is impracticable and, if rigidly applied, would 'shut up every schoolhouse' — it would exclude vast domains (history, philology, geography, political economy, etc.). It is criticized as applying a scientific legalistic test unsuited to education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and condemnation of dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dogmatism — that is, arrogance of opinion, and the disposition to pronounce confidently upon matters that are incapable of being known or verified"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogmatism and undue license of speculation are always condemned; the trait is fostered by certain social agencies (churches, Sunday-schools, religious newspapers) which enforce passive acceptance of unverifiable dogmas. Authors should warn against encouraging dogmatism while criticizing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science begins with questioning and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Science, on the contrary, begins with questioning, and, by insisting upon evidence, has restricted the sphere of speculation"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational practice should reflect science's method of questioning and insistence on evidence rather than passive acceptance; scientific instruction ought to cultivate critical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must teach interpretation and theory, not just facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "What are facts good for if not interpreted, and what is science without explanation — that is, theory?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating education as pouring bare facts into pupils is a 'deadening and paralyzing process.' The highest object of education is to rouse mental activity and encourage independent observation and reflection; linking instruction to explanatory theories and current movements of thought is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for introducing evolution into schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution should be introduced into schools 'simply whether there is sufficient truth and value in it to make its introduction into the schools an improvement upon their existing practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evolution is true at least in its general view and useful as a unifying principle across disciplines, it should be taught; it already appears in geology textbooks and will appear in revised manuals of zoology, botany, psychology, philology, and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of science includes hypotheses and tracing consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: "Science either enjoys perfect liberty, or she is not free at all. Setting up hypotheses and tracing their ultimate consequences are part and parcel of science,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting up and following hypotheses is intrinsic to science and must be part of the liberty of education; hypotheses stimulate research and are indispensable even when later shown to be untenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial aim of scientific research
rubrics_metrics.description: "Scientific research aims at the discovery of truth, never inquiring who is to be benefited thereby. The question, Qui prodest? ... is of as little account in science as ... Cui nocet?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should pursue truth for its own sake, uninfluenced by who benefits or who is hurt; both warners against speculation and speculative investigators are necessary, but progress commonly comes from bold hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should link methods to great movements of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The editors state the importance of 'linking educational methods to the great movements of thought that are absorbing the world's attention, outside of the schools.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To quicken mental activity, curricula should engage with contemporary scientific ideas and methods rather than reduce instruction to rote acquisition of isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of applying scientific oath-tests to humanities and other subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a 'swearing-test' that admits only what a teacher could swear to would exclude most material in history, philology, geography, political economy, and the round of studies already pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a rigid standard is educationally inappropriate; many legitimate subjects rely on interpretation, theory, and best available evidence rather than oath-able certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for a modern treatise on chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' aim: 'to place before the reader a fairly complete and yet a clear and succinct statement of the facts of modern chemistry, while at the same time entering so far into a discussion of chemical theory as the size of the work and the present transition state of the science permit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special attention should be paid to: accurate description of important technical processes; careful representation of the most approved forms of apparatus (with photographic illustrations from apparatus actually in use); proportions adapted for students seeking a thorough general knowledge; clear typography and numerous high-quality illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical merit criterion for medical treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical treatise's chief merit can lie in being 'thoroughly practical' and in comprising lectures on common forms of disease which the author had occasion to deal with in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works grounded in clinical experience, with extensive illustrations of anatomy, instruments, and operations, are especially valuable for practitioners and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for good historical scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Lecky's stated object: 'to disengage from the great mass of facts those which relate to the permanent forces of the nation, or which indicate some of the more enduring features of national life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical writing should focus on deeper causes and enduring influences (growth/decline of institutions, social and economic changes, influences that modified national character) rather than mere year-by-year narration, military events, or trivial incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for encyclopedic/reference works (music dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work 'promises to be... a cyclopaedia of music, giving full and accurate information in regard to the lives of eminent composers, the history of musical instruments, the origin and gradual development of musical forms...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main articles should be contributed by eminent authorities; minor parts prepared with assiduous care; the work should be printed clearly, include musical passages to illustrate topics, and be organized so as to serve both specialists and general readers as a reference and study resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about misleading terminology and analogies in therapeutic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding 'vital magnetism' the editors advise that the term 'magnetism' is 'both fanciful and misleading' and that analogies (e.g., between bodily effects and magnetic charging/discharging) are apt to be carried too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and practitioners should avoid fanciful or misleading names and overextended analogies; present evidence and cases with judgment, avoid sensationalism, and do not paradedetailed claims without proper clinical context (e.g., avoid publishing identifying patient addresses).
